blocks.text: Transitions of electrons in hydrogen and other light elements give spectral lines in the infrared, visible or ultraviolet, because the energy differences between their levels are small. In heavy atoms the electrons are arranged in concentric shells labelled K, L, M, N, O and so on, with the K shell closest to the nucleus (Fig 20.3). The inner-shell electrons are tightly bound, and a large amount of energy is needed to remove them. When an excited atom returns to its normal state, photons of large energy are emitted: transitions of inner-shell electrons in heavy atoms give high-energy photons, X-rays. These X-rays have specific wavelengths and are called characteristic X-rays; their study played a very important part in understanding atomic structure and the periodic table. Fig 20.4 shows where X-rays lie in the electromagnetic spectrum.

blocks.alt: A nucleus surrounded by four dashed circular shells K, L, M and N. An incident high-energy electron comes in from the lower left and strikes an electron in the K shell; the K electron leaves upwards (Ejected electron) and the incident electron goes off to the right (Scattered electron).
blocks.caption: Figure 20.3: Concentric energy shells (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 20.3).

blocks.alt: The electromagnetic spectrum as a coloured band with a wave whose wavelength shortens to the right, labelled from left: radio waves, microwaves, infrared radiation, visible light (a narrow strip), ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma-rays, with small pictures of a radio, a microwave oven, a remote control, a bulb, the Sun and a radiation sign. Scale in metres: 10^3, 1, 10^-3, 10^-5, 10^-7, 10^-9, 10^-11.

blocks.text: X-rays are produced in a high-vacuum X-ray tube (Fig 20.5). The cathode C is heated by a filament F and emits electrons, which are accelerated towards the anode T. If V is the potential difference between C and T, the maximum kinetic energy with which an electron strikes the target is (K.E.)max = Ve (20.1). These fast electrons strike a target of tungsten or another heavy element, and some knock out electrons from the innermost shells, K or L. If a K-shell electron is removed, leaving a hole, an electron from the L shell jumps into the hole, emitting a photon called a K-alpha X-ray: h f(K-alpha) = EL - EK (20.2). An electron from the M shell may fill the hole instead, giving a K-beta X-ray: h f(K-beta) = EM - EK (20.3). These photons from inner-shell transitions are called characteristic X-rays, because their energies depend on the target material. The holes created in the L and M shells are filled by electrons from higher levels, giving more X-rays. The characteristic X-rays appear as discrete lines on a continuous spectrum (Fig 20.6).

blocks.alt: An evacuated glass tube. On the left the cathode C holds a coiled filament (Filament); dotted electron beams cross the tube to a sloping tungsten target (Tungsten anode) mounted in a block with cooling channels on the right. Wavy X-rays leave the target face downwards out of the tube.
blocks.caption: Figure 20.5: Arrangement for producing X-rays (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 20.5).

blocks.text: The continuous spectrum is due to bremsstrahlung, or braking radiation. When the fast electrons strike the target they are suddenly slowed down, and an accelerating (decelerating) charge emits electromagnetic radiation. The deceleration is so large that the radiation has short wavelengths, in the X-ray region. If an electron loses all its kinetic energy in the first collision, the whole of it becomes a single X-ray photon of energy h f_max: (K.E.)max = h f_max. This corresponds to the shortest wavelength, lambda_min, in Fig 20.6. Other electrons lose their energy in several collisions, giving photons of smaller energy (longer wavelength), so a continuous spectrum results.

blocks.alt: A graph of intensity against wavelength (nm) with ticks 0, 0.04, 0.08 and 0.12. The curve is zero up to lambda-min at 0.04 nm, rises to a shoulder, shows two sharp peaks near 0.057 and 0.063 nm, and then falls slowly at longer wavelengths.
blocks.caption: Figure 20.6 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 20.6).

blocks.text: As X-rays travel through the body they lose energy by interacting with atoms; this is called attenuation. X-rays can ionise atoms, knocking out electrons, which is how energy is transferred. The intensity of the beam falls exponentially with the thickness of material: I = Io e^(-mu x), where Io is the initial intensity, I the intensity after passing through the material, x the thickness (in metres) and mu the attenuation coefficient, which depends on the material and the X-ray energy. Image intensifiers are used in real-time X-ray imaging (fluoroscopy); they brighten the image and so reduce the radiation exposure.

blocks.title: Contrast
blocks.text: Contrast in an X-ray image is how clearly different tissues can be told apart. It depends on how differently the tissues absorb X-rays, which depends on their density, thickness and atomic number, and on the X-ray energy.

Hard X-rays (high energy) are used for imaging bone; soft X-rays (low energy) are better for soft tissues such as the breast. Contrast media are substances such as iodine (Z = 53) or barium (Z = 56) that absorb X-rays well; they are injected or swallowed to highlight certain parts of the body. Because of their high atomic numbers they increase X-ray absorption and make those tissues stand out clearly.
